Title: View through a window may influence recovery from surgery
Abstract: Records of patients recovering from cholecystectomy in a suburban hospital were examined to compare patients assigned to rooms with windows facing a natural scene with those facing a brick wall. Patients with the tree view had shorter postoperative stays, fewer negative evaluative comments from nurses and took fewer strong analgesics.

Title: The restorative benefits of nature: Toward an integrative framework
Abstract: Proposes an integrative framework linking directed attention fatigue and the restorative qualities of natural environments, and relates attention restoration to stress recovery.

Authors: Berman M.G., Jonides J., Kaplan S.
Title: The cognitive benefits of interacting with nature
Abstract: Two experiments tested attention restoration theory. Walking in an arboretum, and viewing pictures of nature, improved directed-attention performance compared with walking in or viewing urban environments.

Authors: Roe J.J., Thompson C.W., Aspinall P.A., Brewer M.J., Duff E.I., Miller D., Mitchell R., Clow A.
Title: Green space and stress: Evidence from cortisol measures in deprived urban communities
Source title: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
Abstract: In adults not in work living in deprived urban areas of Scotland, a higher percentage of green space in the living environment was associated with lower perceived stress and a steeper diurnal decline in salivary cortisol.

Authors: Gascon M., Triguero-Mas M., Martínez D., Dadvand P., Forns J., Plasència A., Nieuwenhuijsen M.J.
Title: Mental health benefits of long-term exposure to residential green and blue spaces: A systematic review
Source title: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
Abstract: Systematic review of 28 studies on long-term exposure to residential green and blue spaces and mental health. Limited evidence for a causal relationship between surrounding greenness and mental health in adults; inadequate evidence for children and for blue spaces.

Authors: Bratman G.N., Hamilton J.P., Hahn K.S., Daily G.C., Gross J.J.
Title: Nature experience reduces rumination and subgenual prefrontal cortex activation
Source title: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
Abstract: Healthy urban participants randomly assigned to a 90-minute walk in a natural setting reported less rumination and showed reduced subgenual prefrontal cortex activity compared with those who walked in an urban setting.

Title: The health benefits of the great outdoors: A systematic review and meta-analysis of greenspace exposure and health outcomes
Abstract: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 143 studies. Greenspace exposure was associated with lower salivary cortisol, heart rate and diastolic blood pressure, lower incidence of type II diabetes and better self-reported health.

Authors: White M.P., Alcock I., Grellier J., Wheeler B.W., Hartig T., Warber S.L., Bone A., Depledge M.H., Fleming L.E.
Title: Spending at least 120 minutes a week in nature is associated with good health and wellbeing
Abstract: In a nationally representative sample of about 20,000 adults in England, spending at least 120 minutes a week in nature was associated with higher likelihood of reporting good health and high wellbeing.

Authors: Engemann K., Pedersen C.B., Arge L., Tsirogiannis C., Mortensen P.B., Svenning J.-C.
Title: Residential green space in childhood is associated with lower risk of psychiatric disorders from adolescence into adulthood
Source title: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
Abstract: Using Danish registry data for nearly one million people and satellite-derived greenness, children who grew up with the lowest levels of green space had a higher risk of developing a range of psychiatric disorders later in life.

Title: Environment and crime in the inner city: Does vegetation reduce crime?
Abstract: In inner-city Chicago public housing, buildings with more vegetation had fewer reported property and violent crimes than buildings with less vegetation.

Title: The memory function of sleep
Abstract: Review of the evidence that sleep supports the formation of long-term memory, with emphasis on active systems consolidation during slow-wave sleep.
